classification.difficultyReason: Requires reframing unknown motion as a countable collection of starting-position and jump-size hypotheses, then scheduling each hypothesis at its own future time. The crucial insight is to target its predicted position at that time rather than search fixed locations.

content.prompt: A rabbit moves along the number line. It begins at an integer $n$, and each minute jumps $d$ units to the right (where $d$ is a positive integer). A hunter wishes to trap the rabbit by having it jump into one of her traps. Each minute she can place a trap at any integer value of her choosing. Determine a strategy that will allow the hunter to eventually trap the rabbit, irrespective of the values of $n$ and $d$.

answer.short:
List all pairs $(n_t,d_t)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb N$. Just before the rabbit's $t$th jump, place a trap at $n_t+td_t$.

The actual pair occurs in the list, so its assigned trap catches the rabbit.
answer.worked:
The integers and positive integers are countable. Their Cartesian product is countable, so list every possible pair once as
$$ (n_1,d_1),(n_2,d_2),(n_3,d_3),\ldots. $$
Such a list can be constructed by listing the integers as $0,-1,1,-2,2,\ldots$, arranging pairs with positive integers in a grid, and traversing its diagonals.

Just before the $t$th jump, place a trap at the integer $n_t+td_t$.

The rabbit's actual pair $(n,d)$ occurs at some finite position $T$ in the list. After its $T$th jump, its position is
$$\begin{align*} n+Td&=n_T+Td_T. \end{align*}$$
This is exactly the position of the trap placed for that jump. Hence the strategy eventually catches the rabbit for every integer $n$ and positive integer $d$.
